newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries end lower on late selling wave. [CORRECTED 21:38 GMT]
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries end lower on late selling wave. [CORRECTED 21:38 GMT]

text.p: A late wave of selling pushed U.S. Treasury prices to end lower on Wednesday, overshadowing a highly successful five-year note auction.
The 30-year bond ended at 98-16/32, down 20/32 from Tuesday. Its yield rose to 6.74 percent from 6.69 percent, its highest level since closing at 6.78 percent on June 12.
Market participants said a seller of $1.0 billion in 10-year notes -- rumored to be a foreign central bank -- caught the market off guard and sent it into a tailspin.
"That put the kibosh on any positive sentiment and countered any enthusiasm on the auction," said Kevin Flanagan, money market economist at Dean Witter Securities Inc.

The market sputtered and struggled to move above water for most of the session. U.S. government debt prices finally rallied after the Treasury announced it sold $11.5 billion five-year notes at 6.298 percent, well below the 6.31-6.32 percent the market had anticipated.
The when-issued five-year note rallied to 6.27 percent before running out of steam and closing at 6.32 percent.

Jim Nealis, head trader at PaineWebber Inc, said the market was caught short. "Dealers expected to buy at (6.31 percent) but were shut out," he said. "It took a three-basis-points move (higher) to get the paper back."

But just when the market was climbing -- with the 30-year at its session high of 98-15/32 -- the large seller came in. Analysts speculated that the seller waited until the market hit its highs before unloading.
"When you looked at the results everything there revealed signs the market would do better," Flanagan said.

Not only was the 6.298 percent stop level on the five-year impressive, the bid-to-cover ratio was a very strong 3.19, well above the 2.28 average of the past five auctions, players noted. Non-competitive bids were deemed average at $549 million.
The successful five-year note auction came after a fair two-year auction on Tuesday.
Activity was described as very choppy, with the market unable to find any direction.
"It is a treacherous time," said Mead Briggs, head of proprietary trading at Credit Suisse First Boston Corp.
"The market looks a bit expensive," Briggs said. "But we don't know where the economy is going. We need new data."
Briggs referred to key economic data beginning with the June purchasing managers' and employment reports due next week.

Economic news on Wednesday was largely shrugged off. But, after the market opnened lower, a 0.6 percent rise in May durable goods orders helped to pare some of those losses. The market, however, fell back to lows after a stronger-than-expected 4.4 percent rise in existing home sales in May to a 4.24 million annual unit rate.

Further weighing on Treasuries late in the session was the selling of Treasuries to buy into the $2.8 billion New Jersey Economic Development Authority multi-tranche global issue, maturing in February, 2029.
Also, a rise in crude oil prices on talk that OPEC was either freezing or cutting production was cited as a minor negative for the market.

Treasuries had begun the session under pressure. A stronger than expected Japanese tankan report led to a sharp selloff in the dollar, spilling over to Treasuries. Players said the tankan renewed fears of a Japanese rate hike.

Late on Wednesday, two-year notes were unchanged at 99-30/32 to yield 6.03 percent. Outstanding five-year notes were down 3/32 at 100-29/32 to yield 6.28 percent and the 10-year note was up 1/32 to 101-22/32 to yield 6.39 percent.
Three-month bill rates were steady at 4.94 percent, six-month rates were up one basis point at 5.08 percent and year bill rates were up one basis point at 5.34 percent.
Early in the session, the market shrugged off a 7.8 percent widening of the U.S. trade deficit in April to $8.36 billion, from a revised $7.76 billion gap in March.
(Corrects with updated prices).
(( -- North American Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867 ))
